name: libcdada
baseline: libstdc++ std::set, std::map and std::list (native C++ code on the same libstdc++)
workload: Insert then erase of a fixed array of uint32_t keys (and of 69-byte and 444-byte structs) into set, map and list, timed with RDTSC ticks and summed over 10 runs, cdada C API versus native std::set/std::map/std::list; the benchmark measures libcdada's wrapper overhead.
claimed_speedup: No speedup claimed. README: 'Reasonable performance - comparable to libstdc++'. Table (ticks, std vs cdada): uint32 set insert 752 vs 746, erase 698 vs 743; uint32 map insert 830 vs 809, erase 722 vs 1009; uint32 list insert 20 vs 28, erase 17 vs 20; 69-byte set insert 1410 vs 1623; 69-byte list insert 42 vs 67, erase 22 vs 40.
compiler_and_flags: libcdada configured with ../configure, doc says -O3; compiler version not stated (standard Debian 10 libstdc++ package); benchmark source test/benchmark.cc
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U 1.80GHz/4.6GHz, 16GB DDR4 2667 MHz, cpufreq governor set to performance
tradeoffs: C API wrapper over libstdc++ containers, so it needs the C++ runtime; default containers support 1-256 byte keys padded to a power of two (custom containers for larger or unpadded keys); not thread-safe; POSIX build with autotools; values are copied by value through a void* API.
caveats: Not a faster-than-std result: the doc is an overhead measurement and cdada is level with libstdc++ only on aligned uint32 set/map inserts (within about 1 percent, in the noise). It is slower on most other rows: uint32 map erase about 1.4x slower and list insert about 1.4x slower (derived from page data), 69-byte list erase about 1.8x slower. Single 'random execution' of one run, no variance given; tick normalisation not stated; compiler version missing; Debian 10 era libstdc++ only (no libc++ or MSVC STL). Kept for the C-callable-from-C++ container wrapper role.

name: libcsv
baseline: FasterCSV (pure-Ruby CSV parser, the ancestor of Ruby's stdlib csv)
workload: Downstream benchmark: Rcsv, a Ruby C extension that wraps libcsv 3.0.3, parsing an unstated CSV input versus FasterCSV (user and real seconds); not libcsv's own benchmark and not a pure C comparison.
claimed_speedup: Rcsv (libcsv backend) 0.060 s user / 0.062248 s real versus FasterCSV 0.580 s user / 0.618837 s real, about 9.9x on real time (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 213 stars; packaged by many distributions as libcsv3; wrapped by the Rcsv Ruby gem
tradeoffs: Streaming ANSI C parser with callbacks, LGPL licence (library, not header-only), no SIMD; the repository itself publishes no throughput numbers.
caveats: libcsv's own README, man page and repo carry no benchmark; the only numbers found are in the README of Rcsv (third-party Ruby wrapper, which also does per-column type conversion on top of libcsv) against a pure-Ruby parser from the Ruby 1.8 era. Input file, hardware, Ruby version and flags are all unstated, so the ratio says little about libcsv against other C or C++ CSV parsers. Last commit 2021-08-20 per the rule for abandoned, though the library is stable and widely packaged. Low confidence: kept only as the single numeric comparison reachable; no C or C++ shootout including libcsv was found.
